books.section: Topic 4.9 The Development of an American Culture, B. European Romanticism and American Culture

stimulus.text: James Fenimore Cooper's Leatherstocking Tales, including The Last of the Mohicans (1826), follow the frontiersman Natty Bumppo through the forests of New York during the wars of the 1700s. Cooper's novels mixed adventure with descriptions of the wilderness, and they sold widely in the United States and in Europe.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 6, Topic 4.9 B: Cooper was perhaps the most successful American romantic writer, and his Leatherstocking Tales, including The Last of the Mohicans (1826), captured the danger and fascination of the frontier experience. Original synthesis, not a quotation.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: The wide popularity of Cooper's novels in Europe best shows which of the following?

options.text: European readers had stopped reading their own writers
options.misconception: Cooper sold well abroad, so it is easy to think he replaced every European writer.

options.text: American frontier stories that won readers abroad as well
The United States had banned British books
options.misconception: American books were now competing with British ones, so it is easy to imagine a ban.

options.text: Cooper wrote mainly to please British critics
options.misconception: Europeans praised Cooper, so it is easy to think he wrote for their approval.

rationales.A: Europeans kept reading Scott and their own writers; Cooper joined them on the shelf, he did not clear it.
rationales.B: The stimulus says the novels sold widely in the United States and in Europe alike.
rationales.C: No ban existed; British books still filled American shelves, which is why Cooper's success mattered.
rationales.D: Cooper wrote American frontier stories; European praise followed the books, it did not shape them.
rationales.general:
1. Stick to what the stimulus says. The novels 'sold widely in the United States and in Europe.'
2. Ask what that proves. An American subject — the frontier — could hold foreign readers too.
Background: Barron's notes that Cooper and Irving were internationally popular.
Remember: sales across an ocean are evidence that a subject travels, not just a book.
